nameStory: The Fourtooth Seapill gets its name from two key features: the four distinctive tooth-like projections on its body, and its amazing ability to roll into a tight ball like a pill when threatened. This rolling behavior is just like its terrestrial cousins, the familiar pill bugs or roly-polies you might find under logs in your backyard!
description: The Fourtooth Seapill is a small marine crustacean that looks like the ocean's version of a pill bug. These oval-shaped creatures are typically less than half an inch long and have segmented, armor-like bodies that can curl into a perfect ball. They're part of the isopod group, which means they have seven pairs of legs and are more closely related to shrimp and crabs than to insects, despite their bug-like appearance.

idTips.label: Four tooth-like projections
idTips.description: Look for four distinctive pointed projections or teeth along the body - these are the signature feature that gives this species its name and separate it from other seapills

idTips.label: Ball-rolling ability
idTips.description: When disturbed, it quickly curls into a tight, smooth ball that feels firm and round between your fingers, just like a tiny marble

idTips.label: Segmented body
idTips.description: The oval body has distinct segments that look like overlapping armor plates, feeling slightly rough and ridged to the touch

idTips.label: Seven pairs of legs
idTips.description: Count the legs when it's walking - you'll see seven pairs of small, jointed legs moving in coordinated waves beneath the body

idTips.label: Marine habitat
idTips.description: Found in saltwater environments, often smelling of sea salt and seaweed, unlike the terrestrial pill bugs found in gardens

habitat: Fourtooth Seapills live in marine environments along New England's rocky coastlines, particularly in tide pools, under rocks, and among seaweed beds in the intertidal zone. They prefer areas with good water circulation and rocky substrates where they can find shelter and food. Look for them in the lower intertidal areas that stay moist even at low tide.

seasonality.spring: Active in warming tide pools as water temperatures rise. This is when they're most easily spotted moving around during low tides, emerging from winter hiding spots.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when they're most abundant and visible. Look for them during the lowest tides when their rocky habitat is most accessible.
seasonality.fall: Still active but beginning to move to deeper, more protected areas as storms become more frequent. Good time to find them under larger rocks and in crevices.
seasonality.winter: Much less visible as they retreat to deeper waters and more protected spots. Rarely seen during this season except in the most sheltered tide pools.

funFact: Despite being called a 'sea pill bug,' the Fourtooth Seapill is actually more closely related to lobsters than to the pill bugs in your garden - they're both crustaceans, while garden pill bugs are land-dwelling relatives that breathe through gills and still need moisture to survive!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other small marine isopods or even young shore crabs. The key difference is the four tooth-like projections and the perfect ball-rolling ability - shore crabs can't roll up, and other isopods lack the distinctive four teeth. Remember: 'Four teeth, rolls neat!'
contextualKnowledge: The name 'pill bug' can be confusing because it's used for both marine species like this one and terrestrial species found in gardens. Marine pill bugs like the Fourtooth Seapill are true aquatic crustaceans, while garden pill bugs are land-adapted crustaceans that still need moisture to breathe through their gills.
compareHints: Since this is the only Sphaeroma species documented in New England waters, compare it with other seapill family members by looking for the distinctive four tooth-like projections - this is the defining feature that separates it from other marine isopods in the region. Other seapills may roll into balls, but they won't have these four characteristic teeth.
